youtube.aciklama:
Where does a hearing aid place speech in the ear? In this lesson we cover how the ISTS test signal was created, how to read thresholds, aided speech and discomfort levels on a speech map, percentiles, and the Speech Intelligibility Index (SII).

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Holube, Fredelake, Vlaming and Kollmeier (2010), Development and analysis of an International Speech Test Signal (ISTS), International Journal of Audiology; IEC 60118-15, Methods for characterizing signal processing in hearing aids with a speech-like signal; ANSI/ASA S3.5-1997, Methods for Calculation of the Speech Intelligibility Index; Dillon, Hearing Aids; Mueller, Ricketts and Bentler, Modern Hearing Aids.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn to verify a hearing aid with a signal that resembles real speech, in other words, speech mapping.
Step by step, we will cover the International Speech Test Signal, or ISTS, speech in the ear, and the Speech Intelligibility Index.

maddeler.metin: A pure tone may seem like noise
Goal: see speech in the ear

cumleler: Today's hearing aids analyze the signal continuously and change their behavior according to what they hear.
Noise reduction, feedback cancellation and compression respond to the type of incoming sound and how it changes over time.
A steady pure tone or continuous noise may be treated as noise by these systems and suppressed.
Compression also responds to the rapid ups and downs of speech differently from a steady signal.
So gain measured with pure tones may not fully reflect what the aid really does to speech.
Speech mapping shows directly where a speech-like signal falls in the ear canal.
The International Speech Test Signal, or ISTS, is a signal developed for measuring hearing aids.
It is made from recordings of six female talkers.
The talkers speak American English, Arabic, Mandarin Chinese, French, German and Spanish.
The recordings were cut into short segments and mixed, so the signal is unintelligible but keeps the rhythm and ups and downs of speech.
Its long-term average speech spectrum, or LTASS, matches the average for female speech.
The signal lasts 60 seconds; the first seconds are left for the aid to settle, and analysis uses the part that follows.

cumleler.yazi: The ISTS and its analysis method are defined in an international IEC standard for hearing aid measurement.
cumleler.ses: The ISTS and its analysis method are defined in an international I E C standard for hearing aid measurement.

cumleler: Each talker read the same short text in her own language: the fable of the North Wind and the Sun.
The recordings were cut into short segments about the length of a syllable.
The segments were mixed across languages and rearranged, so no meaningful sentence remained in any language.
The spectrum of the resulting signal was finally adjusted to the international average for female speech.
The result is a language-independent, speech-like signal that can be used the same way all over the world.

y.ad: Level in the ear canal (dB SPL)

cumleler: On a speech map, everything is shown as sound pressure level in front of the tympanic membrane, in dB SPL.
The red line is the person's hearing thresholds converted to this scale; sounds below the line are not heard.
The dashed line at the top shows the person's discomfort level.
The gray curve is the average level of 65 dB SPL average speech in the unaided ear; its high-frequency part stays below threshold.
The blue curve is the level the same speech reaches with the hearing aid.
In this example, aided speech rises above threshold up to 4000 Hz, but above about 5000 Hz it is still not heard.
So on a single screen we see which part of speech is audible and which part is missing.

y.ad: Level in the ear canal (dB SPL)

cumleler: Speech is not a steady sound; its level changes from moment to moment in every frequency band.
In the standard analysis, the signal is examined in one-third octave bands with short windows of 125 milliseconds.

cumleler.yazi: In each band, peaks are shown as the 99th percentile and soft parts as the 30th; the 65th percentile and long-term average lie between.
For unaided ISTS, the difference between the 99th and 30th percentiles, the dynamic range of speech, is about 30 dB.

cumleler: In a hearing aid with compression this range can narrow, and the narrowing is seen directly on the screen.
The goal is for the soft parts of speech to rise above threshold as much as possible, and for peaks not to exceed the discomfort level.

adimlar.metin: From dB HL to dB SPL

cumleler: First, the person's dB HL thresholds are converted to dB SPL in the ear canal using average or measured ear values.
As we saw in the previous lesson, the probe tube is placed about 5 mm from the tympanic membrane.
The ISTS is usually presented at about 55, 65 and 75 to 80 dB SPL, for soft, average and loud speech.
At each level, the measured average curve is compared with the prescriptive target on the same screen, and channel gains are adjusted.
Finally, the aid's maximum output is checked with a sweep at 85 to 90 dB SPL.
A sweep is used instead of a speech signal for maximum output, because the aim is to capture the aid's strongest output.
On the screen we first ask: is the average of average-level speech above threshold at the important frequencies?
Second, are the peaks of loud speech and the maximum output below the discomfort level?
Third, are the soft, average and loud speech curves separated from each other, or is there too much compression?
Finally, is the curve measured at each level close enough to the prescriptive target?
These four questions show whether the aid is doing its basic job before moving on to fine-tuning.
The Speech Intelligibility Index, or SII, sums up in a single number how much of speech is audible.
The value lies between 0 and 1: 0 means no information is audible, and 1 means all speech information is audible.
In the calculation, the part of speech above threshold is found in each frequency band and multiplied by that band's importance weight.

cumleler.yazi: The calculation method for the index is defined in the American standard ANSI S3.5.
cumleler.ses: The calculation method for the index is defined in the American standard A N S I S three point five.

cumleler.yazi: The SII is not an intelligibility percentage; for example, a value of 0.5 does not mean that half of the words will be understood.

cumleler: Many measurement systems show the SII unaided and aided; the difference sums up the aid's contribution to audibility.
In the SII calculation, not every frequency band carries the same weight.
This graph shows approximately the standard average speech importance weights for the octave bands.
The highest importance is in the 1000 and 2000 Hz bands; together they carry about half of the total information.
The 4000 Hz band also has a share of about one fifth.
The 250 and 8000 Hz bands, by contrast, have small shares.
This is why speech made audible in the mid and high frequencies raises the SII much more than at low frequencies.
The SII is a summary of audibility; on its own it does not tell how much the person will actually understand.
Two people with the same SII may get different results, depending on the state of the cochlea and how the brain processes sound.
For children, there are normative studies showing the aided SII values expected for each degree of hearing loss.
Pushing gain too far to maximize the SII can bring discomfort and feedback; the goal is balance.
So the SII should be interpreted together with match to target and the person's feedback.

y.ad: Level in the ear canal (dB SPL)

cumleler: Now let us look at an example adjustment: after the first fit, average-level speech was measured.
The dashed line shows the prescriptive target, and the gray curve shows the first measurement.
Above 2000 Hz, the measured curve falls clearly below target.
This means that the high-frequency consonants of speech are not audible enough.
When gain is increased in the relevant channels and the measurement is repeated, the blue curve moves closer to target.
After the adjustment, the person is asked how the sound feels, and you check for feedback.

sahneler.metin: Before measuring, ask the person not to talk or move their head. The aid's adaptive features settle in the signal's first seconds; read the result after it settles.
cumleler: A tip from the field: before the measurement starts, remind the person not to talk or move their head.
The person's own voice and conversations in the room mix into the measured speech curve.
The aid's adaptive features, such as noise reduction and compression, settle in the first seconds of the signal.
So interpret the curve not as soon as the signal starts, but after it has settled.
If the result looks unexpected, first check the position of the probe tube and which program the aid is in.

maddeler.metin: ISTS: unintelligible speech from six languages
Percentiles show the range of speech

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that the ISTS is an unintelligible but speech-like test signal made from six female talkers in six languages.
The speech map shows thresholds, aided speech and discomfort level on the same dB SPL screen.
Percentiles show the soft parts and peaks of speech, that is, its dynamic range.
The SII sums up audible speech by band importance between 0 and 1; it is not an intelligibility percentage.

sahneler.soru: Which is true for a person with an SII of 0.5?
secenekler: Part of speech information is audible
sahneler.aciklama: The SII is a summary of _audibility_; it cannot be converted directly into percent correct.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: for a person whose SII is 0.5, which statement is true?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: part of the speech information, weighted by importance, is audible.
The SII is a summary of audibility; it does not mean that fifty percent of words will be understood.
